questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: My main goal of studying abroad was to be able to learn in Spanish again and pick up this language in an academic setting. So I explored different universities across South America. I chose Universidad de Los Andes because it is the best university in Colombia and had a really good interdisciplinary program involving environmental and social issues. Also have always wanted to visit Colombia, a country with a lot of diversity within its culture, people and landscapes.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The Exchange Office at Universidad de los Andes is extremely prepared and attentive to the needs of the incoming students. The main point of contact, Anderson, was always fast to respond through email with any questions we had. Before arrival we had some online talks and received a checklist of the documents we need to have to pass migration procedures

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The first week upon arrival there were many intro talks and activities hosted for exchange students specifically. About the university, teaching style in UniAndes, life in Bogotá, code of conduct, safety, local customs and other general advice. This was really insightful and good way to start the term.  We also were introduced to a group of volunteering local students called 'Hermanos Sin Fronteras' that guided us the whole semester and were in contact with us through a WhatsApp groupchat. They planned events, gave us advice, traveled with us and answered smaller questions (eg. where to get a SIM card, restaurant recommendations, transport information, etc)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
-	The exchange team informed us of one main student accommodation that was within walking distance from campus called CityU so I just signed up in advance to secure a spot. It had a gym, common areas, study areas and lots of restaurants nearby. You could choose the type of apartment: own studio and kitchen or sharing apartment with 2, 3 or 4 people. 
-	If I was to do it again I might not choose that student accommodation specifically because they had some issues with management and payment organization. 
-	There were other student accommodations nearby that were just as good and better managed like TheSpot or LivinnX.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
Food is one of the cheapest things in Colombia. Coming from a European background everything seems really affordable. Food choices around campus were really varied from "menu del dia" (menu of the day), fast-food, street food, fresh fruits, chain restaurants, etc. Meals would be from 10-70 kr max. 
Calle 85 and north up of Bogotá has some fancier food restaurants to go out as well. 
Rappi is a go-to food delivery app that is used a lot by students so at night that was a popular food choice as well.... also really affordable. 
I could cook for myself in the apartment, but the kitchen lacked some basic equipment so would only be 2-3 meals/ week whenever I missed home-cooking.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I would say think about your priorities before you sign up to housing accommodation. It is going to be your home and safe place fro 5-10 months so you want to be comfortable in that space. Think whether you prioritize proximity to campus, living on your own, having your own kitchen, having a double bed, living with other people, being close to public transport, etc

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: -	I received access to a course catalogue from UCPH but it was outdated by 2 years. So when I had to sign up to course at UniAndes I could not find the courses I had previously seen on the catalogue. That was a bit tricky because I had to go through the pre-approval UCPH process again which takes up to 6 weeks.  The course registration at UniAndes is a bit messy because since we are exchange students we go through a separate portal from home students to sign up to courses. You are advised to sign up to as many courses as possible because quite a lot are rejected depending on access requirements and availability. Also the website is a bit glitchy and outdated. Just be prepared to deal with this.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: -	Anderson from the UniAndes exchange office is really understanding and warned us about the trickiness of this process. Although he is not a specialist in each course he can help you with the course registration portal

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: -	I managed to register to 2 out of the 3 courses I wanted. And then for the third course, I picked another one that was also interesting and told UCPH again to go through the course pre-approval.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It is a bit like UCPH course registration portal so you won't be too surprised. Always tricky with these online sign up portals because everyone is on it at the same time due to the limited window and the server crashes from time to time. Just be patient and keep an open mind when signing up to courses. Choose a wide range of them so you don't get disappointed that you did not get into some.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: -	I managed to register to 2 out of the 3 courses I wanted. And then for the third course, I picked another one that was also interesting and told UCPH again to go through the course pre-approval.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
-	It was pretty similar to the style of teaching masters at UCPH. We had to do 3-4 readings/ class and then talk about them in class discussions and relate it to other literature and current issues. A different thing was that most class discussions were related to local context so I had to do extra research and readings to prepare for class. The class discussions involved the whole class rather than small working groups like it's normally done at UCPH. Then lastly, we were graded on our class participation and attendance 10-20% of our total grade. 

-	I know for bachelors it was different teaching style to that of UCPH involving more weekly homework that is more “high-school” like

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
I took 3 courses in total. All in Spanish. All worth 10 ECTS or 4 créditos in Colombia.
-	Ecologia Politica y Justicia Ambiental

-	Teorias Feministas y Cambio Social

-	Debates Contemporaneos del Desarollo

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
-	I really liked all 3. They were courses that are also offered in UCPH or at least similar concepts. 
-	I loved learning about political ecology from a latin American perspective and reading local literature. 
-	Teorias Feministas was an eye-opener about how feminism is lived in other parts of the world and the whole academic history and progress of it. Also related the assignments to films and current issues like the new left-wing Colombian government  
-	Maybe I would say that Debates Contemporaneos del Desarollo was the most difficult one because it had a lot of Colombian public policy context and harder to get engaged with. It was also 80% online and post-Covid it is not ideal cause I wanted to interact more with other students in person

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
To visit some places you have to pay "foreign" fees like museums, clubs, outdoor activities and sightseeing places while the local students paid less. It wasn't a lot of money but just something to keep in mind so it doesn't shock you - a very normal thing in Latin America and has a reason behind it. 
For example, a really beautiful national park by the Caribbean coast called Tayrona National Park the entry fee for locals was around 35000 COP while for foreigners it was over 50000 COP.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food is extremely affordable. Did not spend as much money as expected on it as I had predicted. Even when I ate out and more "pricey" meals 

Also accommodations for when I was travelling. Would be able to pay 30000-70000 COP for a night at a decent hostel. Sometimes even sleeping in hammocks would be great if you don't mind that - 20000 COP / night

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
UniAndes is a private university so the extra curricular activities are incredible. There was all kinds of sports and installations: swimming pool, football fields, tennis and squash courts, a fully equipped gym(with machines, classes, weights). Also golf and horseback riding fields (not in the campus but part of the university and accessible through private university transport).
I was personally part of a sewing class elective and the dance classes such as salsa, bachata and merengue and loved every minute.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Some of the above!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Travel! Get to know Colombia! This country is so diverse it could be a continent. There are so many regions to visit. These are some I visited:
- Eje Cafetero - coffee Region and beautiful enchanting houses. The Cocora Valley is a famous sight
- Desierto de la Tatacoa - old tropical forest that is now a desert
- Cali - the capital of salsa
- Boyacá - go village hopping around all the colonial villages. Villa de Leyva, Raquira, Mongui, Pueblito Boyacense, Tibasosa. You can also see frailejones here  which is an endemic tree and landscape that only happens here in Colombia and the Andes region
- Caribbean Coast - visit historic Cartagena de Indias and other cristal blue beaches Islas del Rosario. Tintipan - personal favorite
- Minca - inland paradise with lots of bird biodiversity
- Parque Tayrona: a 3 hour hike and rewarding beach at the end. Can sleep in hammocks.
- Amazonas - visit by traveling to Leticia and then you are at the midway point between Colombian, Peruvian and Brasilian part of the Amazonas. I went with other exchange people and we stayed with an indigenous family that also is part of a conservation group. Check them out on Instagram:
https://instagram.com/hostal_amazonas_huasi_tuor?igshid=YmMyMTA2M2Y
=
- El Chocó / Pacific Coast: really popular to visit this during whale season in October to be able to go whale-watching. I went at a different time and it was equally beautiful. Kilometers of black sand beaches all to myself. Can go surfing here. I stayed in Nuquí and Coquí and Termales. Good place for surf- can stay in their lodge or just rent out the boards --> Paraisurf Colombia near Guachalito

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
For me that was one of the main priorities to fit in. You have to adapt a bit to the normal customs: people socialize differently. Bars and clubs are less about drinking and more about dancing. 
Be open to ask questions. Colombians were so welcoming and loved when I are curious about their country and their traditions. There is a number of festivos / national days that happen all year around so I tried to join and be a part of those.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: In class just talk and chat to the person sitting next to you and ask questions. Otherwise attend events and try to meet as many locals as possible. Be a part of their daily lives, follow the routine! Go to campus events! Ask questions

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The haggling culture is REAL. Not neccesarily a challenge just to have to adapt to it fast once they see you are a foreigner otherwise you can get scammed really easily. Don't be shy and haggle for the prices in taxis, markets, tours, etc. 

Also a really famous saying there: 'No des papaya' which translates to Don't Give Papaya. This means don't flaunt yourself to much in a way you could expose yourself - just a warning to be Be careful with your jewellery, phone, money and your expensive items.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Colombians are so proud of their food, their culture and have a really strong sense of place that I have not seen in many other parts of the world. They know a lot about where they live specially in rural and nature regions. They want to show you Colombia and they appreciate when you enjoy it.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Adapt - try to speak spanish and to the locals as much as possible. Also outside university. The university is a bubble culture since it's private so talk to people outside of it. 

2. Go to the salsa dance classes at UniAndes with prof. Mauricio. He is a pro and makes them so fun 

3. Explore the whole university and all the events it has. Way more social and campus life than that at UCPH

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Good to have a go-to cross-body bag for when you travel and carry important stuff there. 
Don't carry a lot of cash on you - just what you need that day. 

There are more and more places that take in card as payment so I recommend you get a travel debit card. Safest to do this. I even had it on my phone as Apple Pay so didn't have to take out my whole wallet to pay. Some places charge commissions when you pay by card so have that in mind as well

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Travelling and visiting all the regions outside of Colombia. I learned the most this way.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Time difference and being hard from "home" but easy to adapt once you just accept that it's your life. 

Also sometimes it was hard that life became some different after it turned dark at 6pm and it was not as recommended to walk around freely.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Once in a lifetime experience to do 5 months abroad. Would do it 10 times again

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
